data.name: 3079 -- Block Action RPG
data.detailed_description:
3079 is a futuristic, open-world action first-person role playing game. All areas, buildings, items, quests and characters are randomly generated. You will find unique lands & challenges. I hope you enjoy it![/b]

Please follow Phr00t's Software for giveaways, updates & more!

You arrive on a planet experiencing constant war. It is your duty to find out why the warring factions cannot find peace on their own & hopefully restore it yourself.

Java Requirement

Make sure you have Java 7 Update 45 (or better) installed!
On Windows, if you have trouble, you may need to uninstall other versions of Java.
You can get Java from:

Key Features

  • Trading Cards are here!
  • Practically endless, open-world exploration
  • Futuristic weapons and items procedurally generated for endless character equipment
  • Difficulty that increases as you explore further (don't worry, items get better too!)
  • Fully functional Multiplayer with Twitter integration
  • Procedurally generated quests for rewards and story advancement
  • Fortress building using a construction tool
  • Body-part specific damage calculation and dismemberment: Head Shot!
  • Skill system for things like engineering, charisma and camouflage
  • Different biomes (grassland, mountains, snow, poison, desert, sea etc.)
  • Complete storyline that has a start, middle and end
  • Sloped surfaces and higher polygon models gives the world a new, less "blocky" look
  • Challenging artificial intelligence -- enemies and allies will dodge, follow, inspect sounds etc.
  • 3D effects like anti-aliasing, damage & underwater blurring
  • Soft ray-traced lighting (makes for nice shadows to hide in)
  • A very fast, efficient multithreaded engine for smooth, high FPS gameplay almost completely free of "lag"

reviews.review:
[h1]3079 – A Rough, Strange and Surprisingly Addictive Sandbox RPG[/h1]

[i]I have been gaming since the 1980s, have played thousands of games across PC and consoles, and have written close to 500 Steam Curator reviews. Steam shows nearly 74 hours for me in 3079, so this is not a case of judging it after twenty minutes. I have spent enough time with it to understand both why some players love it and why others immediately give up.[/i]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Not Minecraft with guns[/h2]

The first impression is a procedurally generated block world viewed from first person, but the actual structure is closer to a strange mix of an action RPG, Borderlands-style random loot and an experimental sandbox shooter.

You are dropped onto a planet trapped in a permanent war between factions. You begin allied with one side, but your reputation can change, and it is possible to turn against your original allies. A third threat, the demons, attacks everyone and requires special equipment to defeat.

The world, buildings, characters, items and quests are generated. Difficulty rises as you travel farther from the starting area, but equipment also becomes stronger. The main loop is simple: explore, fight, collect weapons, sell unwanted gear, improve skills and move into more dangerous regions.

It is a game driven by systems rather than carefully scripted scenes.

[h2]Loot, skills and progression[/h2]

Weapons and equipment have different values, colours, weight limits and statistics. Finding a stronger rifle, shotgun, sword, launcher, grappling hook or anti-gravity pack can noticeably change how you play.

There is no conventional ammunition system. Weapons use energy, and stronger equipment requires more of it. This is unusual, but it creates one of the largest balance problems. Early weapons can drain energy so quickly that combat becomes slow, while enemies may recover before you are ready to fire again.

Skills improve through use. Firearms increase by shooting, engineering helps with upgrades, charisma affects followers, camouflage supports stealth, and other skills cover mining and stealing. Some advancement methods are repetitive or counter-intuitive, making progression feel more like exploiting a system than naturally developing a character.

Death is also punishing because you lose a random item. Losing ordinary loot is manageable; losing your best gun or grappling hook can be extremely frustrating.

Despite these flaws, the loot chase kept me playing. There is always another small goal: reach a new region, find equipment that supports more weight, improve a useful weapon or escape with valuable gear.

[h2]Movement is the best part[/h2]

The grappling hook and anti-gravity equipment are easily the most enjoyable mechanics.

The hook lets you cross terrain, climb structures, escape battles and reach floating locations. The anti-gravity pack allows controlled movement through the air. Both have weight limits, so entering stronger regions eventually requires improved versions.

That system can feel artificial because every new area makes old mobility equipment obsolete, but when everything works, movement is where 3079 feels most original. Grappling across a battlefield, landing on a tower and firing into a faction fight is more memorable than the simple graphics suggest.

[h2]Combat, factions and AI[/h2]

Combat is functional rather than polished. There are several weapon categories, body-part damage and dismemberment, but the shooting is stiff. Enemy health, energy requirements and generated weapon statistics can create battles that are either trivial or painfully slow.

Allied characters can follow you, which is useful early in the game. Their AI is unreliable, especially inside buildings or around complicated terrain.

Faction behaviour is unforgiving. Accidentally attacking an ally may turn the entire side against you, and changing allegiance is not always easy to reverse. Consequences are welcome, but the game does not explain them clearly enough before they happen.

Demons add another complication. They require a specific weapon and can interfere with movement from a considerable distance. They are interesting at first but become irritating when they repeatedly interrupt exploration.

[h2]Procedural freedom and repetition[/h2]

Procedural generation is both the greatest strength and weakness.

The world can continue almost endlessly, with stronger enemies, different terrain and newly generated equipment. Biomes include grasslands, mountains, snow, deserts, poison areas and seas.

However, a larger world is not automatically a richer one. Buildings and settlements repeat, while missions usually follow a small set of templates: kill a target, protect someone, destroy an object or hack a computer.

The game has a storyline with a beginning and ending, but it is easy to lose among random missions and exploration. This is not a narrative RPG where characters and handcrafted locations drive the experience. It is a sandbox where players create much of the meaning through equipment, travel and self-chosen goals.

[h2]Building and additional systems[/h2]

3079 includes construction, mining, stealing, vehicles, aircraft and multiplayer. That is an impressive feature list for a game made by one developer, but many parts feel experimental rather than fully developed.

Building has limited value because the game encourages constant travel into higher-level territory. Mining exists, but scavenging weapons from battles is often more profitable. Aircraft can be discovered and hijacked, though their controls and AI are unreliable.

Co-op can make the chaos more enjoyable because another player helps compensate for the weak onboarding and harsh beginning. The store also lists cross-platform multiplayer.

There is a lot here, but the systems do not always connect cleanly.

[h2]Presentation and technical age[/h2]

3079 was released in 2011 and looks older in places. Character models, animations, menus and structures are crude. NPC and building scale can appear inconsistent, and the interface requires patience.

It runs through Java, which supported Windows, macOS and Linux, but Java can also create setup friction on modern computers.

The game still has a distinct identity. The strange models, stark landscapes and futuristic music create a lonely, surreal atmosphere, as though you are exploring an abandoned simulation containing a permanent war. Some players will find this charming; others will find it unacceptable.

[h2]Final verdict[/h2]

3079 is ugly, confusing, repetitive and frequently unbalanced. It is also unusual, creative and capable of producing moments that polished mainstream games would never create in quite the same way.

The grappling hook, anti-gravity movement, faction warfare, generated loot and dangerous exploration kept me returning even when the quest design and progression became tedious.

[b]Recommended for patient players who enjoy rough sandbox RPGs.[/b]

Do not buy it expecting Minecraft, Borderlands or a modern survival game with a clean interface. Buy it because you are curious about a strange procedural action RPG made by one developer and are willing to learn its rules through experimentation.

The later 3089 may be easier to recommend to most players, but 3079 still has a distinctive identity. After nearly 74 hours, I cannot pretend there was nothing here worth playing.
